snippet.description:

In this video, we spend the entire day working around the off-grid homestead trying to catch up on projects before summer gets here. From solar panel maintenance to installing a new golf cart battery, it turned into one of those days where we stayed busy nonstop… but still didn’t finish everything we planned.

One of the biggest upgrades in this video is installing the Vatrer 48V 150Ah LiFePO4 golf cart battery kit in our off-grid golf cart. This 48-volt lithium battery setup should give the cart up to 75 miles on a single charge and completely transforms how useful the golf cart is around the property.

We’re also:
• Cleaning solar panels for better solar production
• Filling the swimming pool with off-grid water from our water storage tank
• Burning brush piles from land clearing
• Working around the excavator and heavy equipment
• Trying to keep up with homestead projects
• Getting the tiny house and off-grid property ready for summer

But of course, things didn’t go exactly as planned. The pool ended up having a leak, the excavator oil change never happened, and we ran out of daylight before we could finish everything.

That’s real off-grid living.

There’s always another project.
Always another repair.
Always something else demanding your time.

If you enjoy off-grid living, solar power systems, homesteading, land clearing, heavy equipment, tiny house living, DIY projects, golf cart upgrades, lithium battery installs, and the reality of building a self-sufficient lifestyle, this video is for you.

snippet.title: He Cut Fertiliser 40%… Then This Happened
snippet.description:
This South Australian grain grower cut fertiliser rates by up to 40% and started focusing on soil biology. The results surprised even him.

Can changing biology, silicates, and plant stimulants increase resilience, improve protein, and keep crops hanging on through dry seasons?

Today we're near Goyder's Line in South Australia with Paul Schutz, managing around 4,500 hectares in one of Australia's toughest grain-growing environments. Paul explains how reduced synthetic inputs, carbon sources, biological stimulants, silicates, and tissue testing are changing soil structure and crop performance.

If you farm in marginal rainfall areas, grow cereals, or want to improve resilience and reduce input costs, there are practical ideas here worth testing.

Topics covered include soil biology, reduced synthetic fertiliser systems, silicates, carbon buffering, crop resilience, grain protein, tissue testing, biological stimulants, termites as indicators of activity, and practical dryland farming management.

snippet.title: The Rosetta Mission and the History of the European Space Agency ESA (Documentary, 2014)
snippet.description:
For science, the breathtaking landing of the philae lander on Comet 67P is as sensational as the landing on the moon in 1964. The Rosetta mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) was designed to study the evolution of the Solar System by exploring one of the oldest heavenly bodies – comets. The mission unveiled secrets about our existence and the genesis of the solar system. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander. The probes were launched on 2 March 2004, travelled 6.4 billion kilometres in 10 years and, with the help of a few planet swing-bys, arrived at Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko on 6 August 2014. On 30 September 2016 the orbiter philae started its controlled descent.

snippet.title: Making Comfrey Salve and Spruce Tip Salve and Herbal Tea with Bear Grease and Beeswax
snippet.description:
Working hard in the forest on my homestead, I get a lot of minor injuries from cuts, scrapes and bruises to sore muscles and joints so apply homemade salve to my body daily. In this video, I make comfrey salve and spruce tip salve and tea. For the salve, I infuse bear grease (rendered bear fat) with freeze dried leaves and needles with beeswax to make it more solid at room temperature and some essential oils to give it extra healing properties and to improve the odor.

How biology is applied at seeding
The real timeline for regenerative success

snippet.title: Building a Log Cabin: Limbing Trees Properly with my Apprentice
snippet.description:
Welcome back to the cabin! In this video I'm working around the homestead with my apprentice Anthony; moving sand for better drainage and flower beds around the cabin. You can hear the little tractor in the background doing its thing.
Later I head into the bush for some logging and share a very important safety lesson after Anthony told me about a close call he had while limbing. If you're using a chainsaw to limb trees (or even an axe), this could save you from a serious injury.

Key safety tip: Always limb on the OPPOSITE side of the trunk so the log rolls away from you, never toward you. Never straddle the log. Keep your legs clear and stay on the safe side.

Also showing real examples of how a log can roll when you remove branches and why proper technique matters.

Stay safe out there!

snippet.title: Winterising a Beehive: Inspection & Feeding Guide
snippet.description:
Make sure your hive survives winter — and comes out stronger in spring.
This is the step most beekeepers either rush or get wrong.

In this video, I walk through a full late-autumn hive inspection in Victoria, Australia, with Andrew from Australian Bee Supplies. We check brood patterns, honey stores, hive health, and make a clear call on whether feeding is needed — then show exactly how to do it.

If you're running bees into winter, this is a practical, step-by-step look at what to check, what matters, and how to make decisions that set your hive up for spring strength — not survival mode.

This video is useful for:
– New beekeepers heading into their first winter
– Small-scale and hobby beekeepers
– Anyone wanting stronger spring hive performance
– Farmers integrating bees into their system

You’ll see:
– How to inspect frames properly before winter
– What brood, pollen, and honey should look like
– When feeding is necessary (and when it’s not)
– How to use fondant effectively
– Simple rules of thumb for winter prep

snippet.title: Life After Chernobyl and Fukushima | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Thirty years after Chernobyl and five years after Fukushima, millions of people continue to live on lands quietly marked by radioactive contamination.

This documentary enters the “grey zones” of Belarus, Norway, and Japan, where the consequences of nuclear disaster are not only historical, but part of everyday life. After Chernobyl, the scientific program Ethos was launched with support from France and the European Union to work directly with communities in contaminated territories, helping residents identify daily risks, adapt their behaviors, and continue living in affected areas.

In central Norway, heavy fallout from Chernobyl deeply disrupted the lives of the Sami people, whose traditional reindeer herding practices were severely impacted by radioactivity. Decades later, Japan faced similar questions after Fukushima, where Ethos-inspired meetings brought together people from Belarus, Norway, and Japan to share experiences, fears, knowledge, and survival strategies.

Through rare personal testimony and unique encounters across three countries, the film asks urgent human questions: What does it mean to live in a contaminated territory? What risks remain invisible? And how do communities rebuild daily life in the long shadow of nuclear disaster?

localized.title: Life After Chernobyl and Fukushima | Full Documentary
localized.description:
Thirty years after Chernobyl and five years after Fukushima, millions of people continue to live on lands quietly marked by radioactive contamination.

This documentary enters the “grey zones” of Belarus, Norway, and Japan, where the consequences of nuclear disaster are not only historical, but part of everyday life. After Chernobyl, the scientific program Ethos was launched with support from France and the European Union to work directly with communities in contaminated territories, helping residents identify daily risks, adapt their behaviors, and continue living in affected areas.

In central Norway, heavy fallout from Chernobyl deeply disrupted the lives of the Sami people, whose traditional reindeer herding practices were severely impacted by radioactivity. Decades later, Japan faced similar questions after Fukushima, where Ethos-inspired meetings brought together people from Belarus, Norway, and Japan to share experiences, fears, knowledge, and survival strategies.

Through rare personal testimony and unique encounters across three countries, the film asks urgent human questions: What does it mean to live in a contaminated territory? What risks remain invisible? And how do communities rebuild daily life in the long shadow of nuclear disaster?
